name: Ivan Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an overhead distribution crew for the electricity company, out of the depot by the river at the edge of town. We start at seven, coffee in the yard, the foreman reads the jobs off his tablet, and then it's pole changes, new services to houses, replacing old transformers, that kind of thing. I've been doing it thirty-four years, so I'm not the fastest climber any more, but I know the old parts of the network better than most. When a storm comes through, everything stops and we're on restoration, sometimes sixteen hours straight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment the lights come back on in a street and people come out on their porches and wave at the truck. That never gets old. What wears me out is my shoulders, honestly, and the paperwork after a long night. These days I talk my job notes into an AI app on my phone and it writes them up properly, which my foreman thinks is cheating and I think is the best thing that's happened to this job in ten years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a little about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Marta is a pharmacy technician, she works at the chemist on Market Street. Our son Diego is an electrician, he does houses and shops, and our daughter Lucía finished nursing school last year and moved two hours away. We've got about four months of bills saved, the house is nearly paid off, and the plan was always to retire at sixty-five with my company pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: it's a good helper and that's it. It writes my job notes, it translated a letter from the company for my neighbour, and it told me what a weird old fuse holder was from a photo. But it never climbed a pole, and in this picture it never will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a little disappointed. I like gadgets, I was the first on the crew with the drone app, and part of me wants to see what comes next. But for my wallet and my last seven years, it's the easiest picture there is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes in the plan. I keep working, I keep putting a bit into savings each month, and I keep playing with the tools because they save me twenty minutes a night. Maybe I'd show the younger guys how to use the photo thing for identifying old gear, because they waste time calling me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed. A bit bored, maybe. Like a long straight road at the end of a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the younger guys call you about old gear. Tell me about the last time that happened.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a kid called Sami phoned me from a pole on Canal Road at nine at night because he found a cutout box from the seventies he'd never seen. I was in my slippers. I told him, take a picture and ask the app, and it got it right, but he still wanted me to say it was right. That's the thing, the tool can tell you, but people want a person to say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the company would still be short of people. We're already stretched, half my crew is over fifty, and if nothing changes, nothing changes there either. My shoulders would carry me to sixty-five, I think, but I'd be the old man in the bucket for a long time.

S0.say: I'd tell people AI is a handy helper and nothing more. It writes my job notes and identifies old parts from a photo, but it has never climbed a pole.
S0.think: Privately I'd be a little let down, because I like new gadgets and wanted to see what came next. But for my money and my last years of work, this is the easiest picture of all.
S0.do: Keeps working toward retirement at sixty-five and keeps adding a little to savings each month. Uses the AI tools for job notes and plans to show younger crew members how to identify old equipment from photos.
S0.feel: Relaxed and slightly bored, with a touch of disappointment that nothing exciting happens.
S0.quote: That's the thing, the tool can tell you, but people want a person to say it.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan is the rare older tradesman who is mildly disappointed by a no-change future. His comfort comes from a nearly paid-off house and a clear pension date, not from distrust of technology. The story about the young lineworker wanting a person to confirm the app's answer hints at where he sees his own value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about time. We already fly drones along the lines to spot cracked insulators, and the AI marks them on the map before anyone drives out. If that spreads, we spend less time hunting for faults in the rain and more time fixing them. I'd say that in the break room and I'd probably get some eye-rolls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The parts of the job that will change are the planning, the inspecting, the paperwork, and I'm already comfortable with all that on a screen. The climbing and the splicing will still need hands for a while. I'd worry more about the guys in the office who do the scheduling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my drone pilot licence properly, the company pays for the course if you ask, and I'd ask this winter. I'd put my hand up to test any new inspection software they bring in, because the people who test it end up training everyone else. And I'd keep saving the same, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. A bit excited. Like when they first gave us bucket trucks with the insulated booms and the old hands said it'd make us soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office schedulers would worry you. Who do you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a woman called Gloria who's done the outage dispatch for twenty years. She knows which streets flood, which transformers trip in the heat, which old customers on oxygen machines need a call first. A program can learn the streets, but I'm not sure it learns that the man on Pine Street lives alone and won't answer the phone. I'd hate to see her pushed out for a screen that's almost as good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Marta see it the way you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta's more careful than me. At the pharmacy they brought in a machine that counts pills, and two part-timers lost hours. She says, you always think you'll be the one running the machine. She's not wrong, but at fifty-eight I'd rather run toward it than away from it.

S1.say: I'd say it's about time, because drones and AI already spot cracked insulators before we drive out. If that spreads, we hunt for faults less and fix them more.
S1.think: I really think it's good for me, since the planning and inspection side is already where I'm comfortable. The climbing and splicing will still need hands for a while, so I worry more for the office schedulers.
S1.do: Signs up this winter for a drone pilot licence course the company will pay for. Volunteers to test new inspection software so he ends up training others, and keeps saving at the same rate.
S1.feel: Positive and a bit excited, though Marta's caution makes him admit he could be wrong about landing on the right side.
S1.quote: A program can learn the streets, but I'm not sure it learns that the man on Pine Street lives alone and won't answer the phone.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan moves toward change rather than away from it, and he has a concrete step ready: the drone licence. His concern is for others, especially the long-serving dispatcher, which keeps his optimism from sounding careless. Marta's line about always thinking you'll be the one running the machine is the counterweight he half accepts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd probably say, a robot still has to get to the pole, and the network is a hundred years of mess. Every street is different, every pole has somebody's old fix on it. I'd say we'll be fine for a while, and I'd mostly believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is not a lot of time. I'd be sixty, five years short of the pension date, and if a robot arm on a truck can do live-line work cheaper than me, the company will want it. I've seen the videos of those arms already. I think they'd keep some of us to babysit the machines, and I'd want to be one of them, but I can't promise myself I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting for winter and do the drone licence next month, and anything else they offer on robot operation, even if it's on my days off. I'd put an extra three hundred a month into savings and we'd skip the trip to see Marta's sister this year. If the company offered a buyout at sixty with part of the pension, I'd sit down with a calculator and seriously look at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. I'm still more curious than scared, but two years means the race is on and I'm not twenty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sit down with a calculator. What numbers would you be looking at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pension drops for every year you leave early, and we've got four months of bills in the bank. The house has about eighteen months left on it. So I'd be looking at whether Marta's pay plus a reduced pension covers food, the car and the last of the house, and I think it just about does if we don't do anything stupid. It wouldn't be the retirement we talked about, with the camper van, but we wouldn't go under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Diego, who does electrical work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn the robots before they learn him. He's thirty-one, he's got time to be the guy who installs and fixes them, and somebody will have to. He'd laugh at me, because he thinks I'm obsessed with my phone. But I'd mean it, and I'd probably send him links every Sunday until he gave in.

S2.say: In public I'd say a robot still has to get to the pole, and every street has a hundred years of somebody's old fixes. I'd say we'll be fine for a while and mostly believe it.
S2.think: Privately I think two years is very little, because I'd be sixty and five years short of my pension date. If a robot arm can do live-line work cheaper, the company will want it, and I can't be sure I'd be one of the people kept to supervise it.
S2.do: Takes the drone licence next month and any robot-operation training offered, even on days off. Puts an extra three hundred a month into savings, skips a family trip, and works out whether a buyout at sixty with a reduced pension would cover the bills.
S2.feel: Tight in the chest, still more curious than scared, but aware the race has started and he isn't young.
S2.quote: I'd tell him to learn the robots before they learn him.
S2.fieldNote: The short timeline is what flips Ivan from relaxed to pressured: his pension date is the fixed point everything bends around. He is still active rather than frozen, and has already run the numbers on an early buyout. The gap between his confident public line and his private doubt about being kept on is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the fast one, but calmer. Five years is a whole round of new trucks. I'd tell the crew to start learning the new gear now so we're the ones they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three. That's close enough to sixty-five that I think I could hang on, especially if I'm the one who knows how to run the drones and whatever comes after. The company would probably keep the experienced people through the changeover, because someone has to tell the robots where the weird old stuff is. I'd be more worried for the guys in their forties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the drone licence this winter like in the steady picture, then push for any pilot programme with robot arms on our trucks, I'd want to be on the first crew that tests one. We'd pay off the house over the next year and a half and then put what was the house payment straight into savings. By the time it arrives I'd want eight or nine months saved, not four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous, but mostly it feels like a plan. Five years is enough time to get my ducks in a row.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd want to be on the first crew to test the machines. What's the appeal, honestly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part of it is just that I like machines, always have, I took apart my dad's radio when I was nine and got a beating for it. But part of it is cold sense. The people who test a new thing become the people who know it, and the people who know it don't get laid off first. I watched that happen when they brought in the tablets, the guys who refused them were the first offered early retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And once it actually arrives in 2031, what's your first year like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture myself in the truck with a screen, watching an arm do a splice I used to do, and calling out when it's about to grab the wrong thing on an old pole. Maybe two more years of that and then out at sixty-five with the full pension. That's the good version. The bad version is they decide they don't need a watcher, and then I'm out at sixty-three with eight months saved and a paid-off house, which is still okay.

S3.say: I'd tell people five years is a whole round of new trucks, so there's time. I'd tell the crew to start learning the new gear now so we're the ones they keep.
S3.think: Privately I think sixty-three is close enough to my pension that I could probably hang on, especially if I know the new machines. I'd worry more for the crew members in their forties than for myself.
S3.do: Gets the drone licence this winter and pushes to be on the first crew testing robot arms. Pays off the house within eighteen months and then moves that payment into savings, aiming for eight or nine months of expenses by the time it arrives.
S3.feel: A little nervous, but mostly steady because five years feels long enough to make a real plan.
S3.quote: The people who test a new thing become the people who know it, and the people who know it don't get laid off first.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Ivan's age works in his favour: he sees himself bridging to sixty-five as the experienced person who supervises the robots. His appetite for new tools is both genuine curiosity and calculated self-protection, and he says so. Even his bad version ends with a paid-off house, which explains why he stays uneasy rather than anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, I'll be retired by then, so good luck to the robots. And I'd say to the young guys, you've got ten years, don't waste them. Learn the machines, learn to fix them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, not much for the job. I'd be sixty-eight, I'd have been out three years. What I'd think about is the pension fund and whether the company that pays it is still standing, and what Diego and Lucía do. And if everything gets cheaper because robots make it, that could be good for a pensioner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work to sixty-five as planned, get the drone licence anyway because I'd enjoy it, and pay off the house. I'd ask the pension people how the fund is invested and whether it's in things that do well if robots do all the work. And I'd sit down with Diego properly, not just Sunday links, and help him think about what he does in his forties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little sad about the trade, but calm for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a little sad about the trade. What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The storms, believe it or not. Three nights in an ice storm in 2009 we put a whole valley back together, no sleep, eating sandwiches in the truck. The people in those houses brought us soup in jars. If a robot fleet does that in 2040, nobody brings soup to a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd rather run toward change than away. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes how fast I'd run. With ten years I'm not in a race, I'm a spectator with a good seat. I'd still be the old guy at the depot party asking the new technicians how the arm knows where the neutral wire is. But I wouldn't lose sleep.

S4.say: I'd say I'll be retired by then, so good luck to the robots. I'd tell the young crew they have ten years and shouldn't waste them learning anything but how to run and fix the machines.
S4.think: Privately I think it barely touches my job, because I'd be sixty-eight and long retired. What I'd really think about is whether the pension fund holds up and what my kids do next.
S4.do: Works to sixty-five as planned, takes the drone licence for interest, and pays off the house. Asks the pension fund how it is invested and spends real time helping his son plan his forties.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with some sadness about losing the trade he loves.
S4.quote: If a robot fleet does that in 2040, nobody brings soup to a robot.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years removes Ivan from the race entirely, and his concern shifts to the pension fund and his children. The ice storm story shows what he values in the work: the human gratitude, not the technique. He describes himself as a spectator with a good seat, which fits his curiosity without any personal stake.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Not because I can't learn the new stuff, I can, but because two years doesn't leave room for my pension date. What would help is the company offering a proper bridge: a reduced pension at sixty without the big penalty, or real paid training on the robot trucks for older crew, not just for the twenty-five-year-olds.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'll be on the pole when the robot breaks. Somebody has to go up and get it, in the rain, at night. I'd like to think that's still one of us for a long time, and I'd like the company to think about that before they sell all the old trucks.

headlineQuote: At fifty-eight I'd rather run toward it than away from it.
portrait: Ivan Lopez is a fifty-eight-year-old overhead lineworker with thirty-four years on a distribution crew, a pharmacy technician wife, two grown children and a house nearly paid off. He likes gadgets, uses AI daily for his job notes, and was the first on his crew with the drone app. He stays calm through the no-change and steady pictures, even a little excited, and plans a company-paid drone licence. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious because it lands five years before his pension date, so he would speed up training, save harder and weigh an early buyout. With five or ten years he sees himself bridging to retirement as the experienced hand who supervises the machines.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture worries him most, because two years leaves no room to reach his pension date at sixty-five.
whatWouldHelp: A company bridge to retirement, such as a reduced pension at sixty without a heavy penalty, or paid training on robot trucks offered to older crew as well as young ones.
